## Learning goals

- Recall why mixture MLE is hard ($\log\sum$) and needs a new algorithm family
- Motivate **latent** $Z$ as compression / semantics / unobserved structure
- Define a latent variable model via marginalization of $P_\theta(x,z)$
- See mixtures / GMMs as latent-variable models (discrete component index)

---

## Before this clicks

Mixture: $P_\theta(v)=\sum_j\alpha_j P_{\theta_j}(v)$.  
Log-likelihood has $\log\sum_j$, blocking easy MLE. Joint / marginal / conditional densities for two RVs.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. From mixtures to a broader family

EM will apply to a large class: **latent variable models**. Mixtures are members; so are many deep generative models (VAEs, diffusion — previewed as future course material). Same algorithmic skeleton, different choices of $P(x,z)$.

### 2. Philosophy: information via compression

High-$d$ $x$ (pixels) often has lower-dimensional **semantics** (digit thickness, face attributes, …). Introducing an unobserved $Z$ is a modeling way to talk about that compressed representation. Latent directions can carry editable semantics (style change stories in class).

We typically do **not** hand-label what each coordinate of $Z$ means; the model discovers structure (representation learning). Dimensionality and distributional form of $Z$ are design choices.

### 3. Mathematical definition

Observed data $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Introduce unobserved $z$ (often $z\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ with $k<d$, but not required; for mixtures $z$ is discrete).

**Latent variable model:** define a joint $P_\theta(x,z)$ and set the observed model to the marginal

$$
P_\theta(x)=\sum_z P_\theta(x,z)
\quad\text{(discrete $z$)},
$$

or

$$
P_\theta(x)=\int P_\theta(x,z)\,dz
\quad\text{(continuous $z$)}.
$$

Once a joint exists, so do $P_\theta(z)$, $P_\theta(x\mid z)$, $P_\theta(z\mid x)$, etc.

### 4. What we estimate

Still care about modeling $P(x)$ (or whatever observed law). With latents we typically estimate **both** parameters $\theta$ **and** structure over $Z$ (a distribution on the latent) — because $z$ values were never observed.

### 5. Mixture as latent variable model

Think of discrete $Z\in\{1,\ldots,M\}$ with $P(Z=j)=\alpha_j$ and $P(x\mid Z=j)=P_{\theta_j}(x)$. Then

$$
P_\theta(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\alpha_j P_{\theta_j}(x),
$$

exactly the mixture. So GMM MLE is latent-variable MLE with a discrete component indicator.

### 6. Parameters for a GMM (bookkeeping)

Estimate $\{\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j\}_{j=1}^{M}$. $M$ remains a hyperparameter. Outer sum in the log-likelihood is over data points; inner sum is over components — different roles.

---

## Worked mini-example

Handwritten digit image $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Let discrete $Z\in\{0,\ldots,9\}$ mean “which digit semantics.” Even without labels, a latent-variable model that recovers $P(Z\mid x)$ is doing unsupervised discovery of digit identity — the lecture’s MNIST-style motivation.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Latent $Z$ is in the dataset | By definition unobserved; we infer distributions over it |
| Must know what $Z$ “means” | Usually unsupervised; interpretation is post hoc |
| Latent models replace density estimation | They **are** a way to parameterize $P_\theta(x)$ via a joint |
| Continuous $Z$ only | Mixtures use discrete $Z$; transformers / VAEs often continuous |

4. Is $k=\dim(z)<d$ required mathematically?
5. Why did mixtures push us into this framework?
